items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reservations"?
options: Systematic disadvantage produced when automated classification reproduces inequalities in its data or design
India's policy of reserving places in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes
A set of computational rules that sorts, ranks or predicts, increasingly used to classify people for credit, policing, welfare or advertising
Moving people or things from one category to another, whether by official decision or by social struggle
items.answer: India's policy of reserving places in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes
items.markingKey: B. "reservations" is India's policy of reserving places in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.

items.stem: Sana writes: "The caste system disappeared when untouchability was abolished in 1950." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Caste remains significant in marriage, politics and discrimination, and reservations are themselves organised by caste categories.
items.markingKey: Caste remains significant in marriage, politics and discrimination, and reservations are themselves organised by caste categories. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why caste persists in contemporary India despite legal abolition of untouchability.
items.answer: Caste is reproduced through endogamous marriage, kinship networks, local politics, occupation and everyday discrimination; it has also become a basis of political mobilisation and of reservation policies. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Caste is reproduced through endogamous marriage, kinship networks, local politics, occupation and everyday discrimination; it has also become a basis of political mobilisation and of reservation policies. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the WhatsApp group of the village youth association, someone posts a photograph of the new temple doors. Prakash, whose family were leatherworkers, writes that his cousins were not allowed to help carry the doors. Within minutes, several members reply with folded-hands emojis; one writes "politics should stay out of the temple". The next morning, Prakash posts a photograph of Ambedkar. That evening the group administrator removes him, then adds him back after his uncle, a schoolteacher respected by all castes, telephones the administrator's father.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Maharashtra, India.

Using evidence from the text, describe what happens in the youth association's WhatsApp group. Organise your answer as a series of clearly separated descriptive points.
items.answer: A photograph of new temple doors is posted; Prakash reports his cousins were not allowed to carry the doors; others reply with folded-hands emojis and "politics should stay out of the temple"; Prakash posts an image of Ambedkar; he is removed by the administrator and then re-added after his uncle telephones the administrator's father.

items.stem: Briefly describe Srinivas's research on the Coorgs and in Rampura and explain what it reveals about change and power in caste.
items.answer: Srinivas observed lower castes adopting vegetarianism, teetotalism and Sanskritic rituals, and a peasant caste dominating village politics through land. Sanskritisation and the dominant caste show caste rank shaped by mobility and material power, not only by ritual purity.
items.markingKey: Context (Srinivas observed lower castes adopting vegetarianism, teetotalism and Sanskritic rituals, and a peasant caste dominating village politics through land.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sanskritisation and the dominant caste show caste rank shaped by mobility and material power, not only by ritual purity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to change and power in caste.

Compare and contrast the role of power in the text with power in one ethnography you have studied, such as Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific. Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: Exclusion from carrying temple doors reflects purity-based exclusion of a formerly "untouchable" leatherworking caste (Dumont); others try to depoliticise it ("politics should stay out"), maintaining hierarchy; Prakash challenges it by invoking Ambedkar, symbol of Dalit rights; removal and re-admission show power operating through networks and respect (the schoolteacher uncle), so caste is contested in new digital spaces. Ethnography – Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918): Holding famous kula valuables and keeping many partners brings renown; chiefs and successful kula men gain status through generosity, so prestige rather than accumulation underpins influence. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "India's policy of reserving places in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes"?
items.answer: reservations
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of reservations.

items.stem: Explain the difference between jati and varna.
items.answer: Varna is the four-fold ideal hierarchy of classical texts; jati refers to the thousands of local endogamous groups through which caste is actually lived, whose ranks are often disputed.
items.markingKey: Varna is the four-fold ideal hierarchy of classical texts; jati refers to the thousands of local endogamous groups through which caste is actually lived, whose ranks are often disputed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Caste is simply a Hindu religious belief and has nothing to do with politics." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Caste is tied to land, power and the state: dominant castes control villages, colonial censuses fixed castes, and caste parties shape modern politics.
items.markingKey: Caste is tied to land, power and the state: dominant castes control villages, colonial censuses fixed castes, and caste parties shape modern politics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Nicholas B. Dirks, Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India (2001), explain how the key concept of power helps us to understand caste hierarchy in South Asia.
items.answer: Colonial knowledge was a technology of rule: classifying Indians by caste helped the state govern, recruit and control, and placed Brahmanical ideals at the centre.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Colonial knowledge was a technology of rule: classifying Indians by caste helped the state govern, recruit and control, and placed Brahmanical ideals at the centre. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reclassification"?
options: Identifying people by physical traits such as fingerprints or iris scans, as in India's Aadhaar system
Moving people or things from one category to another, whether by official decision or by social struggle
Official or social acknowledgement of a group's identity and rights, often sought through legal or political struggle
A set of computational rules that sorts, ranks or predicts, increasingly used to classify people for credit, policing, welfare or advertising
items.answer: Moving people or things from one category to another, whether by official decision or by social struggle
items.markingKey: B. "reclassification" is moving people or things from one category to another, whether by official decision or by social struggle.

items.stem: Explain the difference between recognition and redistribution.
items.answer: Recognition seeks acknowledgement of a group's identity and dignity; redistribution seeks a fairer share of material resources. Movements often seek both.
items.markingKey: Recognition seeks acknowledgement of a group's identity and dignity; redistribution seeks a fairer share of material resources. Movements often seek both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Once a category is official, it cannot be changed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Official categories are regularly revised through politics and law, e.g. the removal of Haitians as an AIDS risk group in 1985 and the recognition of a third gender in India in 2014.
items.markingKey: Official categories are regularly revised through politics and law, e.g. the removal of Haitians as an AIDS risk group in 1985 and the recognition of a third gender in India in 2014. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the regional assembly, the Indigenous delegation from the river villages arrive in feathered headdresses that they rarely wear at home. Their spokesperson, Raimunda, a law graduate, reads out the government's definition: "communities maintaining traditional ways of life". "When we use phones, they say we are no longer Indigenous," she says. "So today we wear what they expect, and tomorrow we will take our land." Afterwards, in the car park, the young men change back into football shirts. Raimunda tells me: "The costume is for them. The land is for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a regional assembly in the Brazilian Amazon.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Farmer's analysis of the "4H" AIDS risk groups shows classification, power and stigma.
items.answer: Early US public health reports listed homosexuals, heroin users, haemophiliacs and Haitians as risk groups, and Haitians suffered discrimination in the United States and a collapse of tourism in Haiti. The category blamed a poor nation for the epidemic and hid the role of structural violence and links with the US; Haitian protests helped remove the category.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "stigma".
items.answer: Erving Goffman's term (1963) for an attribute that discredits a person and reduces them "from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one"

items.stem: Explain why categories change over time.
items.answer: Categories are social products, so they shift with power relations, social movements, legal decisions and new knowledge – e.g. census categories adding mixed-race options or courts recognising third genders.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Categories are social products, so they shift with power relations, social movements, legal decisions and new knowledge – e.g. census categories adding mixed-race options or courts recognising third genders. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why classifications of disease can be political.
items.answer: Labelling a group as a "risk group" (Haitians in 1983) shifts blame onto them, affects tourism, employment and migration, and diverts attention from structural causes, so medical categories carry power.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that classification is primarily a tool of the powerful? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Powerful institutions shape classification most strongly, but categories are also resources for those seeking change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: states and experts create categories to govern (Scott, Dirks); risk-group labels stigmatise the poor (Farmer); marginalised groups use categories for solidarity and rights (Dalit, hijra); everyday classifications are made by everyone. items.stem: Which book (1999) by Geoffrey Bowker and Susan Leigh Star examines classification systems and their consequences?
items.answer: Sorting Things Out
items.markingKey: Sorting Things Out. It analyses the ICD and apartheid race classification.

items.stem: Explain the difference between surveillance and legibility.
items.answer: Legibility is making a population readable through standard categories for governance; surveillance is the continuous monitoring of people's behaviour. Digital systems increasingly combine both.
items.markingKey: Legibility is making a population readable through standard categories for governance; surveillance is the continuous monitoring of people's behaviour. Digital systems increasingly combine both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the International Classification of Diseases analysed by Bowker and Star shows classification as invisible infrastructure.
items.answer: The ICD, maintained by the World Health Organization, standardises causes of death and disease for statistics worldwide. Its categories shape which deaths are counted and funded, and reflect negotiations between national and medical interests, showing that technical classifications carry values.
items.markingKey: Context (The ICD, maintained by the World Health Organization, standardises causes of death and disease for statistics worldwide.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: its categories shape which deaths are counted and funded, and reflect negotiations between national and medical interests, showing that technical classifications carry values. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to classification as invisible infrastructure.

The welfare office in Rotterdam introduced a "risk score" last year. Caseworker Annelies shows me the dashboard: applicants are coloured green, amber or red. "I don't know how it decides," she admits. "But if it's red, I must ask for six extra documents." She points out that many red cases live in two postcodes. Mr Yilmaz, an applicant in red, arrives with a folder of documents in plastic sleeves. "My neighbour told me to bring everything," he says. "The computer does not know us, so we must show it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a municipal welfare office in the Netherlands.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Consider the obligations owed to different people involved in the research.
items.answer: Welfare data and applicants' status are confidential; the anthropologist needs permission from the municipality, consent from applicants and staff, and must avoid making identifiable claims about postcodes that could stigmatise neighbourhoods. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Briefly explain why states need legibility.
items.answer: To tax, conscript, plan and deliver services, states need standardised information about people and land, so they create censuses, surnames and identity cards that simplify local complexity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To tax, conscript, plan and deliver services, states need standardised information about people and land, so they create censuses, surnames and identity cards that simplify local complexity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Digital identification systems benefit everyone equally." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Systems like biometric ID can improve access to services but also exclude those whose fingerprints fail or who lack documents, and raise surveillance concerns.
items.markingKey: Systems like biometric ID can improve access to services but also exclude those whose fingerprints fail or who lack documents, and raise surveillance concerns. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Dirks's Castes of Mind (a historical anthropology of British colonial rule in India) as your example, describe how classification is shown.
items.answer: Dirks argued that caste as a rigid, all-India system was substantially shaped by colonial rule, through censuses (from 1871–1872), ethnographic surveys and legal codes that fixed and ranked castes.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Dirks argued that caste as a rigid, all-India system was substantially shaped by colonial rule, through censuses (from 1871–1872), ethnographic surveys and legal codes that fixed and ranked castes. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Nicholas B. Dirks, Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India (2001), a historical anthropology of British colonial rule in India); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to classification. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "Digital classification is more dangerous than earlier forms of bureaucratic classification." Discuss.
items.answer: Digital classification intensifies old dangers of legibility through scale and opacity, but the underlying problem of power over categories is not new.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: algorithms work at huge scale and are opaque; data are combined across systems for surveillance. Arguments against: earlier paper classifications (apartheid, colonial censuses, Rwandan ID cards) caused immense harm; digital systems can be audited and regulated. Supported judgement: Digital classification intensifies old dangers of legibility through scale and opacity, but the underlying problem of power over categories is not new. items.stem: In 2014 the Supreme Court of India, in the NALSA judgment, recognised:
options: transgender people, including hijras, as a "third gender"
items.answer: transgender people, including hijras, as a "third gender"
items.markingKey: A. National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014).

items.stem: Who led the struggle for Dalit rights and chaired the drafting committee of India's Constitution?
items.answer: B. R. Ambedkar
items.markingKey: C. Ambedkar, himself a Dalit, opposed caste and later converted to Buddhism (1956).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "infrastructure (classification)"?
options: Systematic disadvantage produced when automated classification reproduces inequalities in its data or design
Bowker and Star's idea that established classifications become invisible background systems that shape action
Challenging or disputing a category, its boundaries or its meaning, often by those who are disadvantaged by it
India's policy of reserving places in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes
items.answer: Bowker and Star's idea that established classifications become invisible background systems that shape action
items.markingKey: B. "infrastructure (classification)" is Bowker and Star's idea that established classifications become invisible background systems that shape action.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a category imposed from above and a category claimed from below.
items.answer: An imposed category is defined by states, experts or dominant groups for their purposes (colonial caste tables); a claimed category is adopted and redefined by members themselves for solidarity and rights (Dalit identity).
items.markingKey: An imposed category is defined by states, experts or dominant groups for their purposes (colonial caste tables); a claimed category is adopted and redefined by members themselves for solidarity and rights (Dalit identity). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Sanskritisation shows that caste ranking is not completely fixed.
items.answer: Lower castes can rise in local estimation by adopting vegetarianism, Brahmanical rituals and other high-caste customs over generations, showing that caste position is negotiated and changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Lower castes can rise in local estimation by adopting vegetarianism, Brahmanical rituals and other high-caste customs over generations, showing that caste position is negotiated and changes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between legibility and surveillance.
items.answer: Legibility is making a population readable through standard categories for governance; surveillance is the continuous monitoring of people's behaviour. Digital systems increasingly combine both.
items.markingKey: Legibility is making a population readable through standard categories for governance; surveillance is the continuous monitoring of people's behaviour. Digital systems increasingly combine both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Contesting a category always means rejecting it completely." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Groups may also rework a category's meaning or use it strategically, as in strategic essentialism.
items.markingKey: Groups may also rework a category's meaning or use it strategically, as in strategic essentialism. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between Dirks's view of caste and Dumont's view of caste.
items.answer: Dumont saw caste as an enduring religious ideology of hierarchy based on purity; Dirks saw its modern form as a product of colonial power and knowledge.
items.markingKey: Dumont saw caste as an enduring religious ideology of hierarchy based on purity; Dirks saw its modern form as a product of colonial power and knowledge. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why bureaucratic categories can "torque" people's lives.
items.answer: When a person's complex biography does not fit official categories (e.g. a mixed family under apartheid, a migrant without documents), the system forces them into a box with real consequences for rights and relationships.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When a person's complex biography does not fit official categories (e.g. a mixed family under apartheid, a migrant without documents), the system forces them into a box with real consequences for rights and relationships. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the regional assembly, the Indigenous delegation from the river villages arrive in feathered headdresses that they rarely wear at home. Their spokesperson, Raimunda, a law graduate, reads out the government's definition: "communities maintaining traditional ways of life". "When we use phones, they say we are no longer Indigenous," she says. "So today we wear what they expect, and tomorrow we will take our land." Afterwards, in the car park, the young men change back into football shirts. Raimunda tells me: "The costume is for them. The land is for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a regional assembly in the Brazilian Amazon.

Analyse how the delegation contests and uses the government's classification. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: The state defines Indigeneity as "traditional ways of life", which threatens recognition if people modernise. The delegation strategically performs the expected image (strategic essentialism) to claim land rights while privately living modern lives, showing classification as a resource in a power struggle and showing identity as both performed and real.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The state defines Indigeneity as "traditional ways of life", which threatens recognition if people modernise. The delegation strategically performs the expected image (strategic essentialism) to claim land rights while privately living modern lives, showing classification as a resource in a power struggle and showing identity as both performed and real. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Using Srinivas's research on the Coorgs and in Rampura as an example, explain change and power in caste.
items.answer: Srinivas observed lower castes adopting vegetarianism, teetotalism and Sanskritic rituals, and a peasant caste dominating village politics through land. Sanskritisation and the dominant caste show caste rank shaped by mobility and material power, not only by ritual purity.
items.markingKey: Context (Srinivas observed lower castes adopting vegetarianism, teetotalism and Sanskritic rituals, and a peasant caste dominating village politics through land.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sanskritisation and the dominant caste show caste rank shaped by mobility and material power, not only by ritual purity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to change and power in caste.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The welfare office in Rotterdam introduced a "risk score" last year. Caseworker Annelies shows me the dashboard: applicants are coloured green, amber or red. "I don't know how it decides," she admits. "But if it's red, I must ask for six extra documents." She points out that many red cases live in two postcodes. Mr Yilmaz, an applicant in red, arrives with a folder of documents in plastic sleeves. "My neighbour told me to bring everything," he says. "The computer does not know us, so we must show it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a municipal welfare office in the Netherlands.

Explain how the risk score illustrates the relationship between classification and power, using one or more anthropological concepts. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: An opaque algorithm classifies applicants, and even the caseworker cannot explain it, so power lies in the system's categories; clustering of red cases in two postcodes suggests algorithmic bias reproducing spatial and ethnic inequality; applicants adapt (Mr Yilmaz's folder), making themselves legible to "the computer", which shows classification shaping behaviour and identity.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: An opaque algorithm classifies applicants, and even the caseworker cannot explain it, so power lies in the system's categories; clustering of red cases in two postcodes suggests algorithmic bias reproducing spatial and ethnic inequality; applicants adapt (Mr Yilmaz's folder), making themselves legible to "the computer", which shows classification shaping behaviour and identity. items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example Nanda's Neither Man nor Woman, explain the relevance of classification to struggles over social categories.
items.answer: The hijra case challenges the assumption that sex/gender classification is everywhere binary.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The hijra case challenges the assumption that sex/gender classification is everywhere binary. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the WhatsApp group of the village youth association, someone posts a photograph of the new temple doors. Prakash, whose family were leatherworkers, writes that his cousins were not allowed to help carry the doors. Within minutes, several members reply with folded-hands emojis; one writes "politics should stay out of the temple". The next morning, Prakash posts a photograph of Ambedkar. That evening the group administrator removes him, then adds him back after his uncle, a schoolteacher respected by all castes, telephones the administrator's father.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Maharashtra, India.

Identify and describe what happens in the youth association's WhatsApp group. Refer closely to the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: A photograph of new temple doors is posted; Prakash reports his cousins were not allowed to carry the doors; others reply with folded-hands emojis and "politics should stay out of the temple"; Prakash posts an image of Ambedkar; he is removed by the administrator and then re-added after his uncle telephones the administrator's father.

items.stem: Briefly describe the recognition of hijras as a "third gender" in India (NALSA, 2014) and explain what it reveals about how categories are transformed.
items.answer: After activism by transgender and hijra groups, the Supreme Court recognised a third gender and ordered welfare measures. A culturally long-standing but marginalised category gained legal recognition through contestation, though activists debate whether the category fits all transgender people.

items.stem: "Purity and impurity are the key to understanding caste." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Purity is central to caste ideology, but power and economic relations are equally important for its practice.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Dumont's argument; commensality and marriage rules; occupational pollution (leatherwork, sweeping); land, labour and political power also determine rank (Srinivas); Dalit perspectives stress exploitation over purity. Suitable ethnographies include Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus, Dirks's Castes of Mind, Srinivas's work on Sanskritisation and the dominant caste. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Purity is central to caste ideology, but power and economic relations are equally important for its practice. items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Geoffrey Bowker and Susan Leigh Star, Sorting Things Out: Classification and Its Consequences (1999) and Nicholas B. Dirks, Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India (2001).
items.answer: Bowker and Star's Sorting Things Out (on classification systems such as the International Classification of Diseases and apartheid South Africa's race classification): Under apartheid, the Population Registration Act (1950) assigned every person a race, and reclassification decisions determined where people could live, work and marry. Dirks's Castes of Mind (a historical anthropology of British colonial rule in India): Colonial knowledge was a technology of rule: classifying Indians by caste helped the state govern, recruit and control, and placed Brahmanical ideals at the centre. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "varna".
items.answer: The four-fold ranking of Hindu society in classical texts: Brahmin (priests), Kshatriya (warriors and rulers), Vaishya (merchants) and Shudra (labourers), with "Untouchables" outside the system

items.stem: In Seeing Like a State, James C. Scott uses which concept for practical, local knowledge that state schemes ignore?
items.answer: Mētis
items.markingKey: D. Mētis is practical knowledge gained through experience.

items.stem: Explain the difference between redistribution and recognition.
items.answer: Recognition seeks acknowledgement of a group's identity and dignity; redistribution seeks a fairer share of material resources. Movements often seek both.
items.markingKey: Recognition seeks acknowledgement of a group's identity and dignity; redistribution seeks a fairer share of material resources. Movements often seek both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Dirks challenged Dumont's account of caste.
items.answer: Dumont presented caste as an ancient, religious system based on purity; Dirks argued that colonial censuses and ethnography made caste the central, rigid category of Indian society, so caste's modern form is historical and political rather than timeless.

items.stem: Distinguish between a census category and an algorithmic category.
items.answer: A census category is a publicly defined, relatively stable official classification used for counting populations; an algorithmic category is often hidden, dynamic and inferred from behaviour data, and can change without people knowing.

items.stem: With reference to India's Aadhaar biometric identity system, explain how it illustrates digital classification and power.
items.answer: More than a billion residents were enrolled with fingerprints and iris scans, and Aadhaar was linked to food rations, banking and welfare. It made the population legible to the state and widened access for some, while fingerprint failures excluded some poor workers from rations, and critics raised privacy concerns, leading to a 2018 Supreme Court ruling limiting its compulsory use.

items.stem: Briefly describe the International Classification of Diseases analysed by Bowker and Star and explain what it reveals about classification as invisible infrastructure.
items.answer: The ICD, maintained by the World Health Organization, standardises causes of death and disease for statistics worldwide. Its categories shape which deaths are counted and funded, and reflect negotiations between national and medical interests, showing that technical classifications carry values.

At the regional assembly, the Indigenous delegation from the river villages arrive in feathered headdresses that they rarely wear at home. Their spokesperson, Raimunda, a law graduate, reads out the government's definition: "communities maintaining traditional ways of life". "When we use phones, they say we are no longer Indigenous," she says. "So today we wear what they expect, and tomorrow we will take our land." Afterwards, in the car park, the young men change back into football shirts. Raimunda tells me: "The costume is for them. The land is for us."

items.stem: Compare and contrast how classification is shown in Louis Dumont, Homo Hierarchicus: The Caste System and Its Implications (1966; English 1970) and Nicholas B. Dirks, Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India (2001).
items.answer: Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus (drawing on Indian textual sources and his fieldwork among the Pramalai Kallar of Tamil Nadu): Dumont argued that caste rests on a single ideological opposition between the pure and the impure, with Brahmins at the top and "Untouchable" castes at the bottom. Dirks's Castes of Mind (a historical anthropology of British colonial rule in India): Dirks argued that caste as a rigid, all-India system was substantially shaped by colonial rule, through censuses (from 1871–1872), ethnographic surveys and legal codes that fixed and ranked castes. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far classification is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Respond to the big question "Are the categories people use to order the world natural or made?" by drawing on bureaucratic and digital classification, the concept of classification and James C. Scott, Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed (1998) or another anthropological text.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies classification explicitly and uses ethnography: Scott argues that states simplify complex local realities into standardised, "legible" categories – surnames, cadastral maps, censuses – in order to tax, conscript and govern. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

With reference to classification, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Farmer's AIDS and Accusation. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: The state defines Indigeneity as "traditional ways of life", which threatens recognition if people modernise. The delegation strategically performs the expected image (strategic essentialism) to claim land rights while privately living modern lives, showing classification as a resource in a power struggle and showing identity as both performed and real. Ethnography – Paul Farmer, AIDS and Accusation: Haiti and the Geography of Blame (1992), in Do Kay, a village in rural central Haiti settled by people displaced by the Péligre hydroelectric dam: In 1983 the US Centers for Disease Control listed Haitians among AIDS "risk groups", a classification that stigmatised Haitians and blamed them for the epidemic. Comparison: similarities and differences in how classification is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: "Caste in India is a colonial invention." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Colonialism transformed and hardened caste but did not invent it; caste has deep roots reshaped by modern power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: colonial censuses fixed and ranked castes (Dirks); colonial law and ethnography privileged Brahmanical texts. Arguments against: caste-like hierarchy and purity rules are documented long before colonialism; Dumont shows deep religious roots; the claim risks denying Dalits' experience of long-standing oppression. Supported judgement: Colonialism transformed and hardened caste but did not invent it; caste has deep roots reshaped by modern power.
